name: Sharpe ratio
brief:
The Sharpe ratio is return per unit of risk: the average excess return divided by its spread, scaled to a year. It is the first number anyone asks about a backtest.

Write `sharpe_ratio(returns, rf=0.0, periods=252)`. It takes periodic returns, an annual risk-free rate and the number of periods in a year.
definition:
Subtract the risk-free rate per period from every return, $x_t = r_t - \tfrac{r_f}{k}$, where $k$ is `periods`. With the mean $\bar x$ and the sample standard deviation $s$ of the $x_t$,

$$\text{Sharpe} = \dfrac{\bar x}{s} \sqrt{k}$$

Return `None` when there are fewer than two returns or when $s = 0$.
constraints: Use the sample standard deviation, dividing by $n - 1$.
Standard library only. NumPy and pandas are not loaded.
All tests share a 5-second time limit.
hint: Build the list of excess returns first. Then compute the mean and the sample standard deviation of that list, check for zero, and scale by `math.sqrt(periods)`.

tests.name: Empty list
tests.why: With no returns there is no ratio. Return `None`.

tests.name: One return
tests.why: One return has no spread. Return `None` when there are fewer than two.

tests.name: No spread
tests.why: Every return is the same, so the standard deviation is 0 and the ratio is undefined. Return `None`, do not divide by zero.

tests.name: Sample standard deviation
tests.why: Divide the squared deviations by $n - 1$. Here that is 1, so $s \approx 0.01414$.

tests.name: Losing strategy
tests.why: A negative average excess return gives a negative ratio. Keep the sign.

tests.name: Risk-free rate
tests.why: Subtract the daily risk-free rate, $0.05 / 252$, from every return before the mean and spread.

tests.name: Monthly returns
tests.why: Use the `periods` you are given. Monthly data scales by $\sqrt{12}$.

tests.name: Monthly with a rate
tests.why: With monthly data the risk-free rate per period is $0.03 / 12$, not $0.03 / 252$.

tests.name: Long series
tests.note: 50,000 daily returns from a seeded random walk
tests.why: This test has 50,000 returns. One pass for the mean and one for the spread is enough.

how: Submit runs 9 hidden tests. A float counts when it is within a relative 1e-9 of the expected value; where the ratio is undefined, only `None` counts.
where: Builds toward 1.1 level 1, NumPy arrays: the same sums vectorised over a whole array.
notes: `rf / periods` turns the annual rate into a rate per period before it is subtracted.
The ratio of a mean to a standard deviation scales with $\sqrt{k}$, because the mean grows with $k$ and the deviation with $\sqrt{k}$.
Checking `var == 0` before dividing returns `None` instead of raising `ZeroDivisionError`.
prelude:
def _walk(n, seed, start, step):
    # Seeded random walk from an integer LCG, so every Python makes the same prices
    x = seed
    p = start
    out = []
    for _ in range(n):
        x = (x * 1103515245 + 12345) % 2147483648
        p = p * (1 + step * ((x % 2001 - 1000) / 1000))
        out.append(p)
    return out


def _returns(prices):
    return [b / a - 1 for a, b in zip(prices, prices[1:])]
